commands.text:
REGION=eu-west-2
LT_NAME=saa-lbas-task12-lt
ASG_NAME=saa-lbas-task12-asg
SG_NAME=saa-lbas-task12-sg
VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-vpcs --region $REGION --filters Name=is-default,Values=true --query 'Vpcs[0].VpcId' --output text)
SUBNETS=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --region $REGION --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_ID --query 'Subnets[0:2].SubnetId' --output text | tr '\t' ',')

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: variables hold the default VPC and two subnet IDs.

commands.text:
SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region $REGION --group-name $SG_NAME --description 'Task 12 launch template lab' --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query GroupId --output text)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region $REGION --group-id $SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0

AMI_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-images --region $REGION --owners amazon --filters 'Name=name,Values=al2023-ami-*-x86_64' 'Name=state,Values=available' --query 'sort_by(Images,&CreationDate)[-1].ImageId' --output text)
echo $AMI_ID

cat > user-data-v1.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
dnf install -y httpd
echo 'Version 1 from launch template' > /var/www/html/index.html
systemctl enable --now httpd
EOF
USER_DATA_V1=$(base64 -w 0 user-data-v1.sh)
aws ec2 create-launch-template --region $REGION --launch-template-name $LT_NAME --launch-template-data "{\"ImageId\":\"$AMI_ID\",\"InstanceType\":\"t3.micro\",\"SecurityGroupIds\":[\"$SG_ID\"],\"UserData\":\"$USER_DATA_V1\"}"

cliSteps.note: Expected: instance refresh starts and replaces old instances.
cliSteps.title: Create version 2 and roll out

commands.text:
cat > user-data-v2.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
dnf install -y httpd
echo 'Version 2 from launch template' > /var/www/html/index.html
systemctl enable --now httpd
EOF
USER_DATA_V2=$(base64 -w 0 user-data-v2.sh)
aws ec2 create-launch-template-version --region $REGION --launch-template-name $LT_NAME --source-version 1 --launch-template-data "{\"UserData\":\"$USER_DATA_V2\"}"
aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --region $REGION --auto-scaling-group-name $ASG_NAME --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=$LT_NAME,Version=2
aws autoscaling start-instance-refresh --region $REGION --auto-scaling-group-name $ASG_NAME --preferences MinHealthyPercentage=50

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: instance refresh starts and replaces old instances.

cliSteps.title: Verify and clean up
cliSteps.warning: Wait for instances to terminate before deleting the security group if deletion fails.

commands.text:
aws autoscaling describe-instance-refreshes --region $REGION --auto-scaling-group-name $ASG_NAME --query 'InstanceRefreshes[0].Status' --output text
aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group --region $REGION --auto-scaling-group-name $ASG_NAME --min-size 0 --max-size 0 --desired-capacity 0
aws autoscaling delete-auto-scaling-group --region $REGION --auto-scaling-group-name $ASG_NAME --force-delete
aws ec2 delete-launch-template --region $REGION --launch-template-name $LT_NAME
aws ec2 delete-security-group --region $REGION --group-id $SG_ID
rm -f user-data-v1.sh user-data-v2.sh

concepts.body: A lifecycle hook pauses an instance during launch or termination. This gives scripts or people time to act.
concepts.title: Lifecycle hook

concepts.body: The instance waits before moving to the next lifecycle state. The default wait is one hour.
concepts.title: Wait state

concepts.body: Heartbeat timeout controls how long Auto Scaling waits. You can complete, continue, or abandon the action.
concepts.title: Heartbeat timeout

concepts.body: Hook typeWhen it pausesCommon useContinue actionLaunchBefore InServiceInstall software or register appComplete lifecycle actionTerminateBefore TerminatedDrain logs or notify systemComplete lifecycle action
concepts.title: Lifecycle hook plan

examTraps.body: Lifecycle hooks pause the lifecycle. They do not replace unhealthy instances by themselves.

examTraps.title: Trap 2

cheatSheet.body: CONTINUE = move on after timeout. ABANDON = stop the lifecycle action. Use carefully.

cheatSheet.body: CompleteLifecycleAction tells ASG to continue. Use it after the script finishes.
cheatSheet.title: Complete action

cheatSheet.body: Lifecycle hook can trigger EventBridge. EventBridge can trigger Lambda. Lambda can finish setup.

cheatSheet.body: Question says pause launch or termination. Answer is lifecycle hook.

cheatSheet.body: Auto Scaling cooldown = pause after scaling. Cooldown is most linked to simple scaling. Cooldown reduces repeated scale actions.
cheatSheet.title: Cooldown memory

cheatSheet.body: Instance warmup = new instance settling time. Warmup avoids counting fresh instances too soon. Warmup helps target tracking and step scaling.
cheatSheet.title: Warmup memory

cheatSheet.body: Health check grace period = boot protection. It gives new instances time to start. Without it, slow apps may be replaced early.
cheatSheet.title: Health grace memory

cheatSheet.body: Target tracking = keep a metric near a target. Example: CPU near 50 percent. It is simpler than step scaling.
cheatSheet.title: Target tracking choice

cheatSheet.body: Simple scaling = older style. Cooldown matters more here. Use step or target tracking in most exam designs.
cheatSheet.title: Simple scaling choice

cheatSheet.body: Scale out should be fast enough. Warmup stops new capacity being counted too early. Do not set warmup too low for slow apps.
cheatSheet.title: Scale-out behaviour

cheatSheet.body: Scale in should be careful. Too much scale in can hurt availability. Use load balancer draining when targets are removed.
cheatSheet.title: Scale-in behaviour

cheatSheet.body: CPU is common, but not always best. Use request count for web traffic when needed. Use custom metrics for app-specific load.
cheatSheet.title: Metric trap

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Data Model and Schema Flexibility

instructions.text: Use Amazon RDS or Aurora when your application requires complex SQL queries, multi-table `JOIN` operations, or strict relational ACID compliance.
Use Amazon DynamoDB when your application requires flexible JSON schemas, simple key-value lookups, or document storage without relational constraints.

consoleSteps.note: DynamoDB scales horizontally automatically across SSD partitions.
consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Scaling and Latency Requirements

instructions.text: Use DynamoDB when read/write latency MUST remain under 10 milliseconds regardless of data volume or traffic growth.
Use Aurora when you need maximum relational SQL throughput (up to 15 Read Replicas with sub-10ms replication lag).
Use RDS for standard corporate relational database engines requiring moderate scaling.

consoleSteps.note: Global Tables provide active multi-Region writing; Aurora Global Database provides single-writer multi-region reads.
consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Multi-Region Availability Strategy

instructions.text: Choose DynamoDB Global Tables for multi-Region Active-Active read/write capabilities.
Choose Aurora Global Database for multi-Region Active-Passive relational disaster recovery (< 1 second cross-region replication lag).
Choose RDS Cross-Region Replicas for standard asynchronous relational backup read replicas.

consoleSteps.title: Evaluate High Availability and Storage Architecture

Review DynamoDB Multi-AZ: Built-in multi-AZ synchronous storage replication.

concepts.body: RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after a disruption. It is a business requirement, not an automatic guarantee. Lower RTO requires more expensive architectures.
concepts.title: Recovery Time Objective (RTO)

concepts.body: RPO is the maximum acceptable data-loss window, measured in time before the failure. Lower RPO requires more frequent backups or synchronous replication. Asynchronous cross-region replication does not provide zero RPO.
concepts.title: Recovery Point Objective (RPO)

concepts.body: The lowest-cost strategy. Infrastructure may need to be fully recreated after a disaster. RTO and RPO are typically the highest of the four strategies. Restore procedures must be tested regularly.
concepts.title: Backup and Restore

concepts.body: Core services (such as a minimal database replica or AMI) remain running at minimal scale. Other resources are provisioned during recovery. Provides lower RTO than backup-and-restore at moderate cost.
concepts.title: Pilot Light

concepts.body: A scaled-down but fully functional environment runs continuously. Recovery involves scaling up capacity. Provides faster RTO than pilot light at higher ongoing cost.
concepts.title: Warm Standby

concepts.body: Multiple full-scale production environments actively serve traffic simultaneously. Provides the lowest RTO (near-zero) and RPO at the highest cost and operational complexity. Requires data replication and conflict resolution.
concepts.title: Multi-Site Active-Active

examTips.text: SAA-C03: Know the four DR strategies in order of cost and RTO/RPO: Backup & Restore (cheapest, slowest) → Pilot Light → Warm Standby → Multi-site Active-Active (most expensive, fastest).
SAA-C03: RTO and RPO are business requirements. AWS services and architectures can achieve them, but AWS does not automatically guarantee any specific RTO or RPO value.
SAA-C03: Cross-region asynchronous replication (Aurora Global, DynamoDB Global Tables, S3 CRR) does not provide zero RPO. In-transit data may be lost during a regional failure.

examTraps.body: High availability reduces downtime during partial failures (e.g. AZ failure). Disaster recovery restores service after a major failure. They are complementary but distinct concepts.
examTraps.title: DR ≠ HA

examTraps.body: The SAA exam may offer "use Cross-Region Replication for zero RPO" as a trap. Asynchronous replication always has some lag. Only synchronous writes (rare cross-region) could achieve near-zero RPO.
examTraps.title: Asynchronous Cross-Region Replication Is Not Zero RPO

examTraps.body: Backup-and-restore requires restoring the snapshot AND recreating or reconfiguring the surrounding infrastructure. Test the full restore process, not just snapshot creation.
examTraps.title: Backup-and-Restore Is Not Just Snapshots

cheatSheet.body: Backup & Restore: lowest cost, highest RTO/RPO. Pilot Light: core runs, medium cost. Warm Standby: reduced environment runs, lower RTO. Multi-site Active-Active: all runs, lowest RTO, highest cost.
cheatSheet.title: DR Strategy Comparison

cheatSheet.body: RTO = How long can you be down? RPO = How much data can you lose? Both are business decisions, not technical defaults.
cheatSheet.title: RTO vs RPO

cheatSheet.body: Cross-region async replication (Aurora Global, DynamoDB Global Tables, S3 CRR) provides near-zero RPO but not zero RPO. In-flight data may be lost during a regional failure.
cheatSheet.title: Async Replication Caveat

content.memoryHook: DR tiers = Cost vs speed trade-off. Backup-and-Restore is cheapest but slowest. Pilot Light keeps the fire alive. Warm Standby is already dressed for work. Multi-site Active-Active has two offices open simultaneously.
content.costWarning: Multi-AZ and Multi-Region architectures can create charges for duplicate compute, storage, networking, data transfer, load balancing and monitoring resources. Pilot light and warm standby environments incur ongoing costs for their running resources.

instructions.text: Open Amazon RDS -> Choose Create database.

instructions.text: For Homogeneous migrations (e.g. MySQL to RDS MySQL): Use native mysqldump or pg_dump to export and import schema directly.
For Heterogeneous migrations (e.g. Oracle / SQL Server to PostgreSQL / Aurora): Download and launch AWS SCT.
Create a new SCT project -> Connect to Source DB -> Connect to Target RDS DB.
Choose Convert Schema -> Review Schema Transformation Report -> Choose Apply to database.

consoleSteps.note: The replication instance runs the DMS engine that reads source logs and writes to the target.
consoleSteps.title: Create AWS DMS Replication Instance

instructions.text: Open Database Migration Service (DMS).
In the left sidebar, click Replication instances -> Choose Create replication instance.
Set Name to saa-dms-instance.
Set Replication instance class to dms.t3.micro (Free Tier eligible).
Select your VPC and replication subnet group.
Keep Multi-AZ set to Single-AZ to avoid extra charges.
Choose Create replication instance.

consoleSteps.title: Create Source and Target DMS Endpoints

instructions.text: Open DMS -> Endpoints -> Choose Create endpoint.
Source Endpoint: Choose Source endpoint -> Set Identifier saa-source-endpoint -> Engine MySQL -> Input Source IP/DNS, Port 3306, username, and password -> Choose Test endpoint connection.
Target Endpoint: Choose Target endpoint -> Set Identifier saa-target-endpoint -> Check Select RDS DB instance -> Choose saa-dms-target-db -> Input password -> Choose Test endpoint connection.
Ensure both endpoint connections display successful.

consoleSteps.note: Full load copies initial table contents; CDC streams live binlog transactions continuously.
consoleSteps.title: Create and execute Full Load + CDC Replication Task

instructions.text: Open DMS -> Database migration tasks -> Choose Create task.
Set Task identifier to saa-dms-migration-task.
Select Replication instance saa-dms-instance, Source endpoint saa-source-endpoint, and Target endpoint saa-target-endpoint.
Under Migration type, select Migrate existing data and replicate ongoing changes (Full load + CDC).
Under Table mappings, choose Wizard -> Add selection rule -> Schema % -> Table % -> Action Include.
Choose Create task.
Monitor Task status transitioning: Starting → Full load complete → Replication ongoing.
Perform cutover once CDC latency drops to 0 seconds.

concepts.body: Combines a Partition Key (PK) and Sort Key (SK). Items sharing the same PK form an Item Collection sorted physically by SK.
concepts.title: Composite Primary Key (PK + SK)

concepts.body: Finds items matching a specific Partition Key and optionally filters by Sort Key conditions (e.g. OrderDate >= 2026-03-01). Highly efficient and low RCU.
concepts.title: Query Operation

concepts.body: Reads every item in the entire table sequentially. Consumes high RCU throughput, scales poorly, and should be avoided in production.
concepts.title: Scan Operation

concepts.body: DynamoDB Queries support begins_with, between, >, , >=, and on Sort Key values.
concepts.title: Sort Key Comparison Operators

concepts.body: OperationTarget ScopeRCU ConsumptionPerformanceSAA-C03 RecommendationQuerySingle Partition Key (Item Collection)Low (Only matches read)Fast (Primary choice for application lookupsScanEntire Table (All Partitions)High (Evaluates all items)Slow (Linear degradation)Avoid except for small maintenance audits

examTraps.body: If an exam scenario describes high latency or throttled read throughput during lookups, replace Scan calls with Query calls.
examTraps.title: Query vs Scan Performance Traps

cheatSheet.body: Partition Key groups items into physical partitions; Sort Key orders items within the item collection.
cheatSheet.title: Composite Key (PK + SK)

cheatSheet.body: Requires Partition Key. Reads only matching items within the partition collection. Fast and cost-efficient.
cheatSheet.title: Query Operation

cheatSheet.body: Reads entire table partition by partition. Expensive, slow, and consumes RCU heavily.
cheatSheet.title: Scan Operation

content.memoryHook: Query = Targeted & Cheap | Scan = Table-Wide & Expensive | Sort Key = Order & Range

values.label: Required permissions summary
values.value: VPC/subnet setup, Internet Gateway route, EC2 launch, security group setup, IP comparison, and dependency-order cleanup.

cliSteps.title: Create VPC and subnets

commands.text:
REGION=eu-west-2
VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --region $REGION --cidr-block 10.23.0.0/16 --query 'Vpc.VpcId' --output text)
aws ec2 create-tags --region $REGION --resources $VPC_ID --tags Key=Name,Value=saa-ec2-task23-vpc
PUBLIC_SUBNET_ID=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --region $REGION --vpc-id $VPC_ID --cidr-block 10.23.1.0/24 --availability-zone eu-west-2a --query 'Subnet.SubnetId' --output text)
PRIVATE_SUBNET_ID=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --region $REGION --vpc-id $VPC_ID --cidr-block 10.23.11.0/24 --availability-zone eu-west-2a --query 'Subnet.SubnetId' --output text)

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: you create one VPC and two subnets.

cliSteps.note: Expected: instances launched in this subnet can auto-receive public IPv4 addresses.
cliSteps.title: Enable public IP on the public subnet
cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: instances launched in this subnet can auto-receive public IPv4 addresses.

cliSteps.note: Expected: public subnet has a default route to the Internet Gateway.
cliSteps.title: Create Internet Gateway route

commands.text:
IGW_ID=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --region $REGION --query 'InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId' --output text)
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --region $REGION --internet-gateway-id $IGW_ID --vpc-id $VPC_ID
RT_ID=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --region $REGION --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query 'RouteTable.RouteTableId' --output text)
aws ec2 create-route --region $REGION --route-table-id $RT_ID --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id $IGW_ID
aws ec2 associate-route-table --region $REGION --route-table-id $RT_ID --subnet-id $PUBLIC_SUBNET_ID

consoleSteps.note: Lazy Loading ensures only actively requested records consume cache memory.
consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Lazy Loading (Cache-Aside) Code Pattern

instructions.text: Review Lazy Loading logic flow:
1. App queries Redis: `data = redis.get(user_id)`
2. If `data` exists (Cache Hit), return `data` immediately.
3. If `data` is null (Cache Miss), query RDS database: `data = db.query(user_id)`.
4. Save to Redis with TTL: `redis.setex(user_id, 3600, data)`.
5. Return `data` to user.

consoleSteps.note: Write-Through avoids stale cache data at the cost of additional write latency.
consoleSteps.title: Evaluate Write-Through Caching Code Pattern

instructions.text: Review Write-Through logic flow:
1. App updates data: `db.update(user_id, new_data)`
2. App immediately updates Redis: `redis.set(user_id, new_data)`.
3. Subsequent reads hit Redis directly with zero chance of stale data.

commands.text:

cliSteps.title: Create HTTP redirect and HTTPS listener

commands.text:
export HTTPS_LISTENER_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-listener --region $AWS_REGION --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN --protocol HTTPS --port 443 --certificates CertificateArn=$CERT_ARN --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=$TG_ARN --query 'Listeners[0].ListenerArn' --output text)
export HTTP_LISTENER_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-listener --region $AWS_REGION --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN --protocol HTTP --port 80 --default-actions 'Type=redirect,RedirectConfig={Protocol=HTTPS,Port=443,StatusCode=HTTP_301}' --query 'Listeners[0].ListenerArn' --output text)

cat > /tmp/task8-user-data.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
dnf install -y httpd
systemctl enable --now httpd
echo 'HTTPS lab target' > /var/www/html/index.html
EOF
export AMI_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-images --region $AWS_REGION --owners amazon --filters 'Name=name,Values=al2023-ami-*-x86_64' 'Name=state,Values=available' --query 'sort_by(Images,&CreationDate)[-1].ImageId' --output text)

aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group --region $AWS_REGION --auto-scaling-group-name $ASG_NAME --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=$LT_NAME,Version='$Latest' --min-size 2 --max-size 2 --desired-capacity 2 --vpc-zone-identifier $SUBNETS_CSV --target-group-arns $TG_ARN --health-check-type ELB --health-check-grace-period 300

aws acm describe-certificate --region $AWS_REGION --certificate-arn $CERT_ARN --query 'Certificate.Status'

cheatSheet.body: ALB = HTTP and HTTPS app routing. GWLB = transparent network inspection.

cheatSheet.body: NLB = ultra-fast TCP or UDP front door. GWLB = sends packets through appliances.

cheatSheet.body: GWLB spreads traffic across appliance targets. This avoids one firewall becoming a choke point.

commands.text:
cat > /tmp/lbas-task2-userdata.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
dnf install -y httpd
systemctl enable --now httpd
AZ=$(curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/placement/availability-zone)
ID=$(curl -s http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/instance-id)
echo "NLB target $ID in $AZ" > /var/www/html/index.html
EOF
export AMI_ID=$(aws ssm get-parameters --region $AWS_REGION --names /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 --query 'Parameters[0].Value' --output text)
export INSTANCE_IDS=$(for S in $SUBNETS; do aws ec2 run-instances --region $AWS_REGION --image-id $AMI_ID --instance-type t3.micro --subnet-id $S --security-group-ids $SG_ID --user-data file:///tmp/lbas-task2-userdata.sh --tag-specifications "ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=${LAB}-web}]" --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text; done)
echo $INSTANCE_IDS

cheatSheet.body: NLB = Network Load Balancer. NLB works at Layer 4. NLB forwards TCP, UDP, TLS, and related traffic.
cheatSheet.title: NLB core idea

cheatSheet.body: ALB = Application Load Balancer. ALB works at Layer 7. ALB understands HTTP and HTTPS request data.
cheatSheet.title: ALB core idea

cheatSheet.body: NLB = choose for TCP or UDP. NLB = choose for very high performance. NLB = choose for static IP needs.
cheatSheet.title: NLB exam choice

cheatSheet.body: ALB = choose for path routing. ALB = choose for host routing. ALB = choose for HTTP headers and query rules.
cheatSheet.title: ALB exam choice

cheatSheet.body: Target group = backend targets. Listener forwards to target group. Health checks run per target group.
cheatSheet.title: Target groups

cheatSheet.body: NLB health checks can use TCP, HTTP, or HTTPS. Healthy targets receive traffic. Unhealthy targets are avoided.
cheatSheet.title: Health checks

cheatSheet.body: NLB can support static IP addresses. ALB uses DNS names. Exam static IP usually points to NLB.
cheatSheet.title: Static IP memory

cheatSheet.body: NLB with TCP 443 can pass encrypted traffic to targets. The target decrypts. Use this when the app must handle TLS itself.
cheatSheet.title: TLS pass-through

cheatSheet.body: ALB can terminate HTTPS. NLB can also use TLS listeners. TCP listener keeps traffic encrypted to the target.
cheatSheet.title: TLS termination

cheatSheet.body: Target security group must allow traffic. NLB can preserve client IP. For this lab, targets allow HTTP from anywhere.

commands.text:
REGION=eu-west-2

commands.text:
ALB_SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region $REGION --group-name $ALB_SG_NAME --description 'ALB SG for LBAS task 1' --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query 'GroupId' --output text)
WEB_SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region $REGION --group-name $WEB_SG_NAME --description 'Web SG for LBAS task 1' --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query 'GroupId' --output text)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region $REGION --group-id $ALB_SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region $REGION --group-id $WEB_SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 80 --source-group $ALB_SG_ID
echo $ALB_SG_ID
echo $WEB_SG_ID

cliSteps.title: Set safe CLI variables

commands.text:
REGION=eu-west-2
VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-vpcs --region $REGION --filters Name=is-default,Values=true --query 'Vpcs[0].VpcId' --output text)
SUBNETS=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --region $REGION --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_ID Name=default-for-az,Values=true --query 'Subnets[0:2].SubnetId' --output text)
AMI_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-images --region $REGION --owners amazon --filters 'Name=name,Values=al2023-ami-2023*-x86_64' 'Name=state,Values=available' --query 'sort_by(Images,&CreationDate)[-1].ImageId' --output text)
echo $VPC_ID
echo $SUBNETS
echo $AMI_ID

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: you see a default VPC ID, two subnet IDs, and an Amazon Linux 2023 AMI ID.

cliSteps.note: Expected: a security group ID is returned.
cliSteps.title: Create the security group

commands.text:
SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region $REGION --group-name saa-ec2-task26-web-sg --description 'HTTP access for task 26' --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query GroupId --output text)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region $REGION --group-id $SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
echo $SG_ID

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: a security group ID is returned.

cliSteps.note: Expected: the instance reaches running state.
cliSteps.title: Launch the EC2 web server

commands.text:
cat > /tmp/task26-user-data.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
dnf install -y httpd
systemctl enable --now httpd
echo 'Hello from EC2 behind ALB and NLB' > /var/www/html/index.html
EOF
INSTANCE_ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --region $REGION --image-id $AMI_ID --instance-type t3.micro --subnet-id $(echo $SUBNETS | awk '{print $1}') --security-group-ids $SG_ID --user-data file:///tmp/task26-user-data.sh --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-ec2-task26-web}]' --query 'Instances[0].InstanceId' --output text)
aws ec2 wait instance-running --region $REGION --instance-ids $INSTANCE_ID
echo $INSTANCE_ID

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: the instance reaches running state.

cliSteps.note: Expected: both target group ARNs are shown.
cliSteps.title: Create ALB and NLB target groups

commands.text:
ALB_TG_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-target-group --region $REGION --name saa-ec2-task26-alb-tg --protocol HTTP --port 80 --vpc-id $VPC_ID --target-type instance --health-check-protocol HTTP --health-check-path / --query 'TargetGroups[0].TargetGroupArn' --output text)
NLB_TG_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-target-group --region $REGION --name saa-ec2-task26-nlb-tg --protocol TCP --port 80 --vpc-id $VPC_ID --target-type instance --query 'TargetGroups[0].TargetGroupArn' --output text)
aws elbv2 register-targets --region $REGION --target-group-arn $ALB_TG_ARN --targets Id=$INSTANCE_ID
aws elbv2 register-targets --region $REGION --target-group-arn $NLB_TG_ARN --targets Id=$INSTANCE_ID
echo $ALB_TG_ARN
echo $NLB_TG_ARN

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: both target group ARNs are shown.

cliSteps.note: Expected: both load balancers become available.
cliSteps.title: Create the ALB and NLB

commands.text:
ALB_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --region $REGION --name saa-ec2-task26-alb --type application --scheme internet-facing --subnets $SUBNETS --security-groups $SG_ID --query 'LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn' --output text)
NLB_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --region $REGION --name saa-ec2-task26-nlb --type network --scheme internet-facing --subnets $SUBNETS --query 'LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn' --output text)
aws elbv2 wait load-balancer-available --region $REGION --load-balancer-arns $ALB_ARN $NLB_ARN
echo $ALB_ARN
echo $NLB_ARN

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: both load balancers become available.

cliSteps.note: Expected: both listener ARNs are shown.
cliSteps.title: Create listeners

commands.text:
ALB_LISTENER_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-listener --region $REGION --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN --protocol HTTP --port 80 --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=$ALB_TG_ARN --query 'Listeners[0].ListenerArn' --output text)
NLB_LISTENER_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-listener --region $REGION --load-balancer-arn $NLB_ARN --protocol TCP --port 80 --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=$NLB_TG_ARN --query 'Listeners[0].ListenerArn' --output text)
echo $ALB_LISTENER_ARN
echo $NLB_LISTENER_ARN

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: both listener ARNs are shown.

cliSteps.note: Open both DNS names in a browser. Expected: the test web page appears.
cliSteps.title: Get load balancer DNS names

cliSteps.note: Expected: load balancers, target groups, instance, security group, and local test file are removed.
cliSteps.title: Clean up
cliSteps.warning: Destructive Command Warning: This command permanently terminates AWS resources, scaling policies, or load balancer configurations.

commands.text:
aws elbv2 delete-listener --region $REGION --listener-arn $ALB_LISTENER_ARN
aws elbv2 delete-listener --region $REGION --listener-arn $NLB_LISTENER_ARN
aws elbv2 delete-load-balancer --region $REGION --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN
aws elbv2 delete-load-balancer --region $REGION --load-balancer-arn $NLB_ARN
sleep 60
aws elbv2 delete-target-group --region $REGION --target-group-arn $ALB_TG_ARN
aws elbv2 delete-target-group --region $REGION --target-group-arn $NLB_TG_ARN
aws ec2 terminate-instances --region $REGION --instance-ids $INSTANCE_ID
aws ec2 wait instance-terminated --region $REGION --instance-ids $INSTANCE_ID
aws ec2 delete-security-group --region $REGION --group-id $SG_ID
rm -f /tmp/task26-user-data.sh

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: load balancers, target groups, instance, security group, and local test file are removed.

NAME=saa-lbas-task-9
VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-vpcs --region $REGION --filters Name=is-default,Values=true --query "Vpcs[0].VpcId" --output text)
SUBNETS=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --region $REGION --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_ID Name=default-for-az,Values=true --query "Subnets[0:2].SubnetId" --output text)
echo $VPC_ID $SUBNETS

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: one default VPC ID and two subnet IDs.

cliSteps.note: Expected: security group ID.
cliSteps.title: Create security group

commands.text:
SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region $REGION --group-name ${NAME}-sg --description "Task 9 ALB stickiness SG" --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query GroupId --output text)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region $REGION --group-id $SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
echo $SG_ID

cliSteps.note: This creates the target group and enables ALB cookie stickiness.
cliSteps.title: Create target group and enable stickiness

commands.text:
TG_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-target-group --region $REGION --name ${NAME}-tg --protocol HTTP --port 80 --vpc-id $VPC_ID --target-type instance --query TargetGroups[0].TargetGroupArn --output text)
aws elbv2 modify-target-group-attributes --region $REGION --target-group-arn $TG_ARN --attributes Key=stickiness.enabled,Value=true Key=stickiness.lb_cookie.duration_seconds,Value=300
echo $TG_ARN

cliSteps.note: Register instances after you launch them, or use the Console for the instance step.
cliSteps.title: Create the ALB

commands.text:
ALB_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --region $REGION --name ${NAME}-alb --type application --scheme internet-facing --security-groups $SG_ID --subnets $SUBNETS --query LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn --output text)
aws elbv2 wait load-balancer-available --region $REGION --load-balancer-arns $ALB_ARN
LISTENER_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-listener --region $REGION --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN --protocol HTTP --port 80 --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=$TG_ARN --query Listeners[0].ListenerArn --output text)
ALB_DNS=$(aws elbv2 describe-load-balancers --region $REGION --load-balancer-arns $ALB_ARN --query LoadBalancers[0].DNSName --output text)
echo http://$ALB_DNS

cliSteps.note: Expected: stickiness is enabled and duration is 300 seconds.
cliSteps.title: Verify stickiness attributes
cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: stickiness is enabled and duration is 300 seconds.

cliSteps.title: Clean up
cliSteps.warning: Terminate any EC2 instances you launched before deleting the security group if deletion fails.

commands.text:
aws elbv2 delete-listener --region $REGION --listener-arn $LISTENER_ARN
aws elbv2 delete-load-balancer --region $REGION --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN
sleep 30
aws elbv2 delete-target-group --region $REGION --target-group-arn $TG_ARN
aws ec2 delete-security-group --region $REGION --group-id $SG_ID

commands.text:
REGION="eu-west-2"; BUCKET="combo-demo-bucket"; USER="cross-demo-user"; PROFILE_TEST="cross"
aws s3api create-bucket --bucket "$BUCKET" --region "$REGION" --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$REGION"
echo "hello" > example.txt
aws s3 cp example.txt s3://$BUCKET/

aws iam create-user --user-name "$USER"
cat > user-read.json <<'JSON'
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Sid":"UserReadObjects","Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::combo-demo-bucket/*"}]}
JSON
aws iam put-user-policy --user-name "$USER" --policy-name UserObjectRead --policy-document file://user-read.json

ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
cat > bucket-policy.json <<JSON
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Sid":"AllowUserList","Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"AWS":"arn:aws:iam::$ACCOUNT_ID:user/$USER"},"Action":"s3:ListBucket","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::$BUCKET"}]}
JSON
aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket "$BUCKET" --policy file://bucket-policy.json

cliSteps.note: Expected: list/get succeed; put fails.

title: Create a permissions boundary and prove it limits permissions

content.goal: Goal: Show that a permissions boundary acts as the maximum permissions for a user, even if another policy tries to allow more.
content.title: Create a permissions boundary and prove it limits permissions

cleanup.text: Detach all managed policies, remove users from groups, and delete test IAM identities created during this lab.

commands.text:
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
aws iam put-user-permissions-boundary \
  --user-name iam-noperms-user \
  --permissions-boundary arn:aws:iam::$ACCOUNT_ID:policy/ReadOnlyBoundaryPolicy

cliSteps.title: Create and attach broad allow policy

commands.text:
cat > allow-readwrite.json <<'EOF'
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Sid": "AllowReadWrite",
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
    "Resource": ["arn:aws:s3:::my-boundary-bucket", "arn:aws:s3:::my-boundary-bucket/*"]
  }]
}
EOF
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
aws iam create-policy --policy-name AllowReadWriteToBoundaryBucket --policy-document file://allow-readwrite.json
aws iam attach-user-policy --user-name iam-noperms-user --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::$ACCOUNT_ID:policy/AllowReadWriteToBoundaryBucket

cliSteps.note: Expected: list works; upload fails.

echo test > b.txt && aws s3 cp b.txt s3://my-boundary-bucket/ --profile noperms

cliSteps.warning: Destructive Command Warning: This command permanently detaches permissions or deletes IAM identity resources.

aws iam delete-policy --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::$ACCOUNT_ID:policy/AllowReadWriteToBoundaryBucket

cliSteps.title: Set variables from your AWS login state

commands.text:
REGION="eu-west-2"
ADMIN_PROFILE="default"
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --profile "$ADMIN_PROFILE" --query Account --output text)
ALLOWED_BUCKET="iam-task-3-allowed-bucket-$ACCOUNT_ID"
BLOCKED_BUCKET="iam-task-3-blocked-bucket-$ACCOUNT_ID"
USER_NAME="iam-task-3-user"
POLICY_NAME="IAMTask3ListOnlyOneBucketPolicy"
TEST_PROFILE="iam-task-3-user"

echo "Account: $ACCOUNT_ID"
echo "Allowed bucket: $ALLOWED_BUCKET"
echo "Blocked bucket: $BLOCKED_BUCKET"

cliSteps.note: The blocked bucket is optional in the scenario, but useful because it proves the policy is scoped to one bucket.
cliSteps.title: Create the two empty S3 buckets

commands.text:
aws s3api create-bucket \
  --bucket "$ALLOWED_BUCKET" \
  --region "$REGION" \
  --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$REGION" \
  --profile "$ADMIN_PROFILE"

aws s3api create-bucket \
  --bucket "$BLOCKED_BUCKET" \
  --region "$REGION" \
  --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint="$REGION" \
  --profile "$ADMIN_PROFILE"

cliSteps.title: Create the policy document
cliSteps.warning: This policy intentionally does not allow s3:ListAllMyBuckets, s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, or access to $BLOCKED_BUCKET.

cliSteps.title: Create and attach the customer managed policy

commands.text:
POLICY_ARN=$(aws iam create-policy \
  --policy-name "$POLICY_NAME" \
  --policy-document file://iam-task-3-policy.json \
  --query Policy.Arn \
  --output text \
  --profile "$ADMIN_PROFILE")

aws iam attach-user-policy \
  --user-name "$USER_NAME" \
  --policy-arn "$POLICY_ARN" \
  --profile "$ADMIN_PROFILE"

echo "Policy ARN: $POLICY_ARN"

cliSteps.warning: The file iam-task-3-access-key.json contains credentials. Delete it during tear down.

aws iam create-access-key \
  --user-name "$USER_NAME" \
  --profile "$ADMIN_PROFILE" \
  --output json > iam-task-3-access-key.json

SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=$(python -c "import json;print(json.load(open('iam-task-3-access-key.json'))['AccessKey']['SecretAccessKey'])")

aws configure set aws_access_key_id "$ACCESS_KEY_ID" --profile "$TEST_PROFILE"
aws configure set aws_secret_access_key "$SECRET_ACCESS_KEY" --profile "$TEST_PROFILE"

title: Lambda stops only tagged EC2 instances

content.goal: Goal: Create a Lambda execution role with least privilege, then prove it can stop only EC2 instances tagged AutoStop=true.
content.title: Lambda stops only tagged EC2 instances

cleanup.text: Detach all managed policies, remove users from groups, and delete test IAM identities created during this lab.

commands.text:
aws configure set region eu-west-2
REGION="eu-west-2"
ROLE_NAME="LambdaEc2TagManagerRole"
FUNC_NAME="stop-tagged-ec2"
TAG_KEY="AutoStop"
TAG_VALUE="true"
SG_NAME="lambda-ec2-test-sg"
KEY_NAME="lambda-ec2-test-key"
RUNTIME="python3.12"

VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-vpcs --filters Name=isDefault,Values=true --query "Vpcs[0].VpcId" --output text)
SUBNET_ID=$(aws ec2 describe-subnets --filters Name=default-for-az,Values=true --query "Subnets[0].SubnetId" --output text)
SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name "$SG_NAME" --description "SG for IAM Task 25" --vpc-id "$VPC_ID" --query GroupId --output text)
aws ec2 create-key-pair --key-name "$KEY_NAME" --query KeyMaterial --output text > "$KEY_NAME.pem"
chmod 400 "$KEY_NAME.pem"
AMI_ID=$(aws ssm get-parameter --name /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/al2023-ami-kernel-default-x86_64 --query Parameter.Value --output text)

TAGGED_ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --image-id "$AMI_ID" --instance-type t3.micro --key-name "$KEY_NAME" --security-group-ids "$SG_ID" --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID" --tag-specifications "ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=tagged-instance},{Key=$TAG_KEY,Value=$TAG_VALUE}]" --query "Instances[0].InstanceId" --output text)
UNTAGGED_ID=$(aws ec2 run-instances --image-id "$AMI_ID" --instance-type t3.micro --key-name "$KEY_NAME" --security-group-ids "$SG_ID" --subnet-id "$SUBNET_ID" --tag-specifications "ResourceType=instance,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=untagged-instance}]" --query "Instances[0].InstanceId" --output text)
aws ec2 wait instance-running --instance-ids "$TAGGED_ID" "$UNTAGGED_ID"

cat > trust.json <<'JSON'
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"lambda.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}
JSON
aws iam create-role --role-name "$ROLE_NAME" --assume-role-policy-document file://trust.json
aws iam attach-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE_NAME" --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole
cat > manage-tagged-ec2.json <<'JSON'
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Sid":"DescribeInstances","Effect":"Allow","Action":"ec2:DescribeInstances","Resource":"*"},{"Sid":"StopOnlyTagged","Effect":"Allow","Action":"ec2:StopInstances","Resource":"arn:aws:ec2:*:*:instance/*","Condition":{"StringEquals":{"ec2:ResourceTag/AutoStop":"true"}}}]}
JSON
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE_NAME" --policy-name ManageTaggedEc2 --policy-document file://manage-tagged-ec2.json

aws lambda invoke --function-name "$FUNC_NAME" --payload '{"mode":"stop"}' response.json
cat response.json
aws lambda invoke --function-name "$FUNC_NAME" --payload "{"mode":"stop","untagged_instance_id":"$UNTAGGED_ID"}" response2.json
cat response2.json
aws ec2 describe-instances --instance-ids "$TAGGED_ID" "$UNTAGGED_ID" --query "Reservations[].Instances[].{Id:InstanceId,State:State.Name,Name:Tags[?Key=='Name']|[0].Value,AutoStop:Tags[?Key=='AutoStop']|[0].Value}" --output table

cliSteps.title: Tear down in dependency order
cliSteps.warning: Destructive Command Warning: This command permanently detaches permissions or deletes IAM identity resources.

commands.text:
aws lambda delete-function --function-name "$FUNC_NAME"
aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE_NAME" --policy-name ManageTaggedEc2
aws iam detach-role-policy --role-name "$ROLE_NAME" --policy-arn arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/service-role/AWSLambdaBasicExecutionRole
aws iam delete-role --role-name "$ROLE_NAME"
aws ec2 terminate-instances --instance-ids "$TAGGED_ID" "$UNTAGGED_ID"
aws ec2 wait instance-terminated --instance-ids "$TAGGED_ID" "$UNTAGGED_ID"
aws ec2 delete-security-group --group-id "$SG_ID"
aws ec2 delete-key-pair --key-name "$KEY_NAME"
rm -f "$KEY_NAME.pem" trust.json manage-tagged-ec2.json lambda_function.py function.zip response.json response2.json

concepts.body: The primary access control mechanism for KMS keys. Unlike S3 or IAM policies, IAM policies alone cannot grant access to a KMS key unless the KMS Key Policy explicitly permits the account/role.
concepts.title: KMS Key Policies

concepts.body: Encrypting plaintext data with a Data Key locally, and then encrypting the Data Key under a master KMS Key (CMK). Essential for encrypting datasets larger than 4 KB.
concepts.title: Envelope Encryption

concepts.body: KMS CMK: Never leaves the HSM hardware; encrypts/decrypts up to 4 KB. Data Key: Generated by KMS; used locally by your application to encrypt large payload data.
concepts.title: Data Keys vs KMS Master Keys

concepts.body: AWS KMS automatically rotates Customer Managed Keys every 365 days, retaining old key versions so existing encrypted data can still be decrypted seamlessly.
concepts.title: Automatic Key Rotation

concepts.body: Key TypeManaged ByRotation OptionsKey Policy ModificationAWS Managed Key (e.g. `aws/s3`)AWS ServicesAutomatic every 3 years (Fixed)No (Read-only policy)Customer Managed Key (CMK)Customer (You)Optional automatic annual (365 days) rotationYes (Full policy customization)AWS Owned KeyAWS InternalManaged internally by AWSNo access

examTraps.body: AWS KMS `kms:Encrypt` API cannot directly encrypt payloads larger than **4 KB (4096 bytes)**. For larger files, choose Envelope Encryption (GenerateDataKey).

concepts.body: RDS uploads daily storage volume backups and continuously archives transaction logs (write-ahead logs) to S3. This combo enables Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) down to a specific second.
concepts.title: Automated Backups & PITR

concepts.body: User-initiated storage volume backups that are retained indefinitely, even after you delete the parent RDS database instance. They never expire automatically.
concepts.title: Manual DB Snapshots

examTips.text: SAA-C03: Master Amazon RDS concepts and multi-AZ / replication design in Amazon RDS.

examTraps.body: Exam questions might suggest that executing PITR or restoring an RDS snapshot overwrites the existing live production database. This is false. Restoring *always* spins up a completely separate database with a new endpoint string.
examTraps.title: The Overwrite Trap

examTraps.body: Be careful: if a question states an instance was terminated and asks how to recover data from an *automated* backup, you can't—unless you specifically checked the box to retain automated backups during deletion. Manual snapshots are the only ones preserved by default.
examTraps.title: Instance Deletion Backup Purge

cheatSheet.body: Automated backups delete automatically when you delete the parent RDS instance. Retention spans from 1 to 35 days. Setting retention to 0 completely disables automated backups and purges PITR history logs.
cheatSheet.title: Automated Backup Lifecycle

cheatSheet.body: Manual snapshots survive database deletion entirely. They remain on AWS storage until you manually log in and delete them.
cheatSheet.title: Manual Snapshot Longevity

cheatSheet.body: PITR references your daily automated backup image + incremental transaction logs to reconstruct an identical instance clone at any given target second within your retention bracket.
cheatSheet.title: Point-in-Time Recovery Mechanics

content.memoryHook: Automated dies with the instance; Manual lives on. Automated backups match the DB instance's lifespan. Manual snapshots stay until *you* say goodbye.

consoleSteps.title: Verify Automated Backup Configuration

instructions.text: Open the RDS Console and click Databases on the left navigation panel.
Click your existing database instance (e.g., saa-db-task5-encrypted-instance).
Select the Maintenance & backups tab.
Under the Backups section, verify that the Backup retention period is set to 1 day or greater.
Note the Latest restorable time timestamp; this represents your closest operational threshold for PITR.
With your database instance still highlighted, click the top Actions menu button.
Select Take snapshot from the context dropdown menu.
In the Snapshot identifier text field, input saa-db-task6-manual-snap.
Click the Take snapshot submission button and wait for its status to change from 'Creating' to 'Available'.

consoleSteps.title: Explore Point-in-Time Recovery Options
consoleSteps.warning: Both Snapshot restoration and PITR do *not* overwrite your running database. They always deploy a brand new, separate DB instance with a fresh endpoint.

instructions.text: Return to the primary Databases inventory sub-menu.
Select your active target instance, click Actions, and pick Restore to point in time.
Observe the configuration wizard: notice you can select either the Latest restorable time or pick a custom Specific time.
Exit this setup screen by clicking Cancel without executing a new deployment spin-up.
Navigate to Snapshots under the left sidebar menu.
Select the radio checkbox for your manual snapshot saa-db-task6-manual-snap.
Click Actions, choose Delete snapshot, and confirm the pop-up warning sequence.

content.whyItMatters: Architecting for disaster recovery requires knowing the trade-offs between automated retention vs. manual persistence. The exam heavily tests RPO/RTO scenarios using these three features.

troubleshooting.body: Cause: Automated backup tracking was disabled (retention period set to 0). Fix: Modify your database properties, change backup retention settings to at least 1 day, and wait for a new backup routine to initialize.

troubleshooting.body: Cause: Attempting to create a snapshot while the parent DB is undergoing hardware modifications or heavy software upgrades. Fix: Wait until the core RDS resource state shifts back to 'Available' before initiating a backup call.

commands.text:
REGION=eu-west-2

cliSteps.title: Find the default VPC

echo $VPC_ID

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: a VPC ID like vpc-123456.

cliSteps.note: Expected: two security group IDs.
cliSteps.title: Create security groups

commands.text:
EC2_SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region $REGION --group-name $EC2_SG_NAME --description 'EC2 client security group for RDS task 1' --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query 'GroupId' --output text)
DB_SG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --region $REGION --group-name $DB_SG_NAME --description 'RDS DB security group for task 1' --vpc-id $VPC_ID --query 'GroupId' --output text)
echo $EC2_SG_ID
echo $DB_SG_ID

cliSteps.title: Add security group rules
cliSteps.warning: The curl command uses an internet service to find your public IP.

commands.text:
MY_IP=$(curl -s https://checkip.amazonaws.com)/32
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region $REGION --group-id $EC2_SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr $MY_IP
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --region $REGION --group-id $DB_SG_ID --protocol tcp --port 3306 --source-group $EC2_SG_ID

cliSteps.note: Expected: RDS accepts at least two subnets.

aws rds create-db-subnet-group --region $REGION --db-subnet-group-name rds-task1-subnet-group --db-subnet-group-description 'RDS task 1 subnet group' --subnet-ids $SUBNETS

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: RDS accepts at least two subnets.

commands.text:

echo

echo $DB_ENDPOINT

concepts.body: RDS storage encryption protects your data, backups, read replicas, and snapshots from unauthorized physical storage access. It uses AES-256 validation mechanisms.

examTraps.body: The exam will ask how to encrypt a production database running without encryption. You *cannot* just click modify. The correct architecture path is: Snapshot the instance -> Copy the snapshot with encryption turned ON -> Restore a new DB from that new encrypted snapshot.

cheatSheet.body: You cannot toggle an existing active RDS database from unencrypted to encrypted. You must create a new encrypted database instance or copy an unencrypted snapshot into an encrypted state.

content.goal: Configure Amazon Route 53 health checks and a failover routing policy to automatically reroute global user traffic away from an unhealthy primary endpoint to a healthy secondary endpoint. Understand how TTL and DNS caching affect failover timing.
content.title: Global Traffic Routing and Health Check Failover with Amazon Route 53

values.label: DNS TTL
values.value: Lower values (e.g. 60s) speed up failover at higher query cost

cleanup.text: Delete all test Route 53 health checks created for this lab.
Remove the failover DNS records (primary and secondary) from the hosted zone.
Delete the hosted zone only if it was created solely for this lab.
Delete CloudWatch alarms and SNS notifications created for health-check monitoring.

concepts.body: Route 53 failover routing policy designates one record as primary and another as secondary. When the primary health check fails, Route 53 returns the secondary record.
concepts.title: Failover Routing Policy

concepts.body: Route 53 health checks monitor endpoints (HTTP, HTTPS, TCP) or other Route 53 health checks (calculated). They run from multiple AWS locations globally.
concepts.title: Health Checks

concepts.body: DNS records have a Time To Live (TTL) value in seconds. Resolvers and clients cache records for this duration. Lower TTLs reduce failover time but increase DNS query costs. DNS failover is not instantaneous.
concepts.title: TTL and DNS Caching

concepts.body: When enabled on alias records, Evaluate Target Health allows Route 53 to follow health checks of the target resource (e.g. load balancer targets) rather than requiring a separate health check.
concepts.title: Evaluate Target Health

concepts.body: The effective Recovery Time Objective (RTO) for DNS failover is influenced by the health check interval, failure threshold, and the TTL of the DNS record. Lower TTL and shorter health-check intervals reduce effective RTO.
concepts.title: RTO vs TTL

examTips.text: SAA-C03: Route 53 failover routing requires a health check on the primary record. When the health check fails, Route 53 returns the secondary record. TTL and resolver caching affect how quickly clients see the change.
SAA-C03: Failover routing is for active-passive DR. For active-active with health-based distribution, consider weighted or latency routing with health checks.

examTraps.body: TTL and resolver caching mean clients may continue resolving to the failed endpoint for the TTL duration even after health check failure is detected. This must be factored into RTO calculations.
examTraps.title: DNS Failover Is Not Instantaneous

examTraps.body: Route 53 health checks cannot directly monitor VPC-internal endpoints. Use CloudWatch alarm-based health checks for internal resources.
examTraps.title: Private Hosted Zones and Health Checks

examTraps.body: Failover routing is for active-passive DR. Weighted routing splits traffic by percentage. Latency routing directs users to the lowest-latency region. Do not confuse them.
examTraps.title: Failover vs Weighted vs Latency Routing

cheatSheet.body: Create a Primary FAILOVER record pointing to your active endpoint with a health check. Create a Secondary FAILOVER record pointing to your DR endpoint. Enable health checks on the primary.
cheatSheet.title: Failover Record Setup

cheatSheet.body: Endpoint health checks: monitor a URL or IP. Calculated health checks: combine results of multiple child health checks. CloudWatch alarm health checks: based on a CloudWatch alarm state.
cheatSheet.title: Health Check Types

cheatSheet.body: Lower TTL before a planned failover or maintenance window. Restore normal TTL afterward to reduce DNS query costs.
cheatSheet.title: TTL Best Practice

content.memoryHook: Route 53 failover = DNS-layer lifeguard. When primary drowns (health check fails), secondary gets the traffic — but clients cached to the old answer still need to wait for their TTL to expire.

commands.text:
aws s3api delete-bucket-lifecycle --bucket $BUCKET
aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket $BUCKET --output json > versions.json
python - <<'PY'
import json, subprocess, os
bucket=os.environ['BUCKET']
data=json.load(open('versions.json'))
items=[]
for v in data.get('Versions',[]):
    items.append({'Key':v['Key'],'VersionId':v['VersionId']})
for m in data.get('DeleteMarkers',[]):
    items.append({'Key':m['Key'],'VersionId':m['VersionId']})
if items:
    payload={'Objects':items,'Quiet':False}
    open('delete-versions.json','w').write(json.dumps(payload))
    subprocess.run(['aws','s3api','delete-objects','--bucket',bucket,'--delete','file://delete-versions.json'],check=True)
PY
aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket $BUCKET --region $REGION

title: Delete a file, then restore it using S3 versioning

content.goal: Goal: Enable S3 Versioning, delete an object, then restore it by removing the delete marker or copying an older version back as the current version.
content.title: Delete a file, then restore it using S3 versioning

commands.text:
REGION="eu-west-2"
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
BUCKET="saa-s3-task-4-versioning-restore-$ACCOUNT_ID"
KEY="versioning-restore-demo.txt"

echo "Bucket: $BUCKET"
echo "Key: $KEY"

cliSteps.note: Expected result: Status should show Enabled.
cliSteps.title: Enable bucket versioning

commands.text:
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning \
  --bucket "$BUCKET" \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket "$BUCKET"

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected result: Status should show Enabled.

cliSteps.title: Create and upload a test file

commands.text:
echo "Version 1 - keep me safe" > versioning-restore-demo.txt

aws s3api put-object \
  --bucket "$BUCKET" \
  --key "$KEY" \
  --body versioning-restore-demo.txt

cliSteps.note: Because versioning is enabled, this creates a delete marker.
cliSteps.title: Delete the object

cliSteps.note: Expected result: the object key should not appear in the normal current object list.
cliSteps.title: Prove the object looks deleted
cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected result: the object key should not appear in the normal current object list.

cliSteps.note: Look for DeleteMarkers. The delete marker is hiding the older object version.
cliSteps.title: Find the delete marker
Restore by deleting the delete marker
cliSteps.warning: This deletes the delete marker, not the old object version.

commands.text:
DELETE_MARKER_VERSION_ID=$(aws s3api list-object-versions \
  --bucket "$BUCKET" \
  --prefix "$KEY" \
  --query "DeleteMarkers[?IsLatest==\`true\`].VersionId | [0]" \
  --output text)

echo "Delete marker version ID: $DELETE_MARKER_VERSION_ID"

aws s3api delete-object \
  --bucket "$BUCKET" \
  --key "$KEY" \
  --version-id "$DELETE_MARKER_VERSION_ID"

cliSteps.note: Expected result: the key appears again and the downloaded file contains your original text.
cliSteps.title: Verify the object is visible again

commands.text:
aws s3api list-objects-v2 \
  --bucket "$BUCKET" \
  --query "Contents[].Key" \
  --output text

commands.text:
DIST_ID=$(aws cloudfront list-distributions --query "DistributionList.Items[?Comment=='S3 Task 16 website distribution'].Id | [0]" --output text)
ETAG=$(aws cloudfront get-distribution-config --id $DIST_ID --query ETag --output text)
aws cloudfront get-distribution-config --id $DIST_ID --query DistributionConfig > cf-config.json
python - <<'PY'
import json

d=json.load(open(p))
d['Enabled']=False
json.dump(d, open(p,'w'))
PY
aws cloudfront update-distribution --id $DIST_ID --if-match $ETAG --distribution-config file://cf-config.json
echo "Wait until disabled and Deployed, then run delete-distribution with the new ETag."

commands.text:
aws s3api delete-bucket-replication --bucket $SOURCE
for B in $SOURCE $DEST; do
  aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket $B --output json > versions-$B.json
  python - <<PY
import json, subprocess
bucket='$B'
data=json.load(open('versions-$B.json'))
items=[]
for v in data.get('Versions',[]):
    items.append({'Key':v['Key'],'VersionId':v['VersionId']})
for m in data.get('DeleteMarkers',[]):
    items.append({'Key':m['Key'],'VersionId':m['VersionId']})
if items:
    open('delete-'+bucket+'.json','w').write(json.dumps({'Objects':items,'Quiet':False}))
    subprocess.run(['aws','s3api','delete-objects','--bucket',bucket,'--delete','file://delete-'+bucket+'.json'],check=True)
PY
done
aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name $ROLE_NAME --policy-name s3-task20-replication-policy
aws iam delete-role --role-name $ROLE_NAME
aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket $DEST --region $REGION
aws s3api delete-bucket --bucket $SOURCE --region $REGION

instructions.text: Open AWS Snow Family Console.

Set Bucket name to saa-snow-migration-vault-[account-id].
Set Region to us-east-1.

Enable Bucket Versioning (recommended for audit trails during large data imports).
Choose Create bucket.

consoleSteps.note: Lifecycle rules automatically transition uploaded data to lowest-cost Glacier storage classes.
consoleSteps.title: Configure S3 Lifecycle Rule for Immediate Glacier Archiving

instructions.text: Select bucket saa-snow-migration-vault-[account-id] -> Choose Management tab.
Click Create lifecycle rule.
Set Lifecycle rule name to ArchiveSnowballImports.
Choose Apply to all objects in the bucket.
Check Move current versions of objects between storage classes.
Select Glacier Deep Archive -> Set Days after object creation to 1 (or minimum allowed).
Choose Create rule.

consoleSteps.note: Fires automated triggers whenever new objects land in the destination S3 bucket.
consoleSteps.title: Configure EventBridge Trigger for Automated Validation

instructions.text: Open Amazon EventBridge -> Choose Rules -> Create rule.
Set Name to catch-snowball-s3-upload.
Select Rule with an event pattern -> Event source AWS services -> Service S3 -> Event type Amazon S3 Event Notification.
Set Target to CloudWatch log group or SNS Topic saa-snow-alerts.
Choose Create rule.

Open Amazon S3 Console -> Open saa-file-gateway-bridge-[account-id].
Verify that hybrid-test.txt appears instantly as a native S3 object.

title: Configure route tables for IGW and NAT

content.goal: Goal: Add a route to an Internet Gateway for public subnets and a route to a NAT Gateway for private subnets.
content.title: Configure route tables for IGW and NAT

values.label: Required permissions summary
values.value: STS identity check, VPC setup, IGW setup, NAT Gateway setup, route table changes, and cleanup.

cleanup.text: Delete subnets, route tables, Internet Gateways, and the custom VPC created during this lab.

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: you see your AWS account ID and ARN.

cliSteps.note: Expected: the public route table targets the IGW, and the private route table targets the NAT Gateway.
cliSteps.title: Create VPC, subnets, IGW, NAT, and route tables

commands.text:
REGION=eu-west-2
VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.60.0.0/16 --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task-6}]' --query 'Vpc.VpcId' --output text)
PUBLIC_SUBNET_ID=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC_ID --cidr-block 10.60.1.0/24 --availability-zone eu-west-2a --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task-6-public-a}]' --query 'Subnet.SubnetId' --output text)
PRIVATE_SUBNET_ID=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC_ID --cidr-block 10.60.11.0/24 --availability-zone eu-west-2a --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task-6-private-a}]' --query 'Subnet.SubnetId' --output text)
IGW_ID=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=internet-gateway,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task-6-igw}]' --query 'InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId' --output text)
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --internet-gateway-id $IGW_ID --vpc-id $VPC_ID --region $REGION
EIP_ALLOC_ID=$(aws ec2 allocate-address --domain vpc --region $REGION --query 'AllocationId' --output text)
NAT_ID=$(aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id $PUBLIC_SUBNET_ID --allocation-id $EIP_ALLOC_ID --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=natgateway,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task-6-nat}]' --query 'NatGateway.NatGatewayId' --output text)
aws ec2 wait nat-gateway-available --nat-gateway-ids $NAT_ID --region $REGION
PUBLIC_RT_ID=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id $VPC_ID --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=route-table,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task-6-public-rt}]' --query 'RouteTable.RouteTableId' --output text)
PRIVATE_RT_ID=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id $VPC_ID --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=route-table,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task-6-private-rt}]' --query 'RouteTable.RouteTableId' --output text)
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $PUBLIC_RT_ID --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id $IGW_ID --region $REGION
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $PRIVATE_RT_ID --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --nat-gateway-id $NAT_ID --region $REGION
PUBLIC_ASSOC_ID=$(aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id $PUBLIC_RT_ID --subnet-id $PUBLIC_SUBNET_ID --region $REGION --query 'AssociationId' --output text)
PRIVATE_ASSOC_ID=$(aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id $PRIVATE_RT_ID --subnet-id $PRIVATE_SUBNET_ID --region $REGION --query 'AssociationId' --output text)
echo $VPC_ID $PUBLIC_RT_ID $PRIVATE_RT_ID $NAT_ID $IGW_ID $EIP_ALLOC_ID $PUBLIC_ASSOC_ID $PRIVATE_ASSOC_ID

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: the public route table targets the IGW, and the private route table targets the NAT Gateway.

cliSteps.note: Look for GatewayId on the public table and NatGatewayId on the private table.
cliSteps.title: Verify routes
Cleanup

aws ec2 delete-nat-gateway --nat-gateway-id $NAT_ID --region eu-west-2

aws ec2 release-address --allocation-id $EIP_ALLOC_ID --region eu-west-2

title: Configure VPC Flow Logs for an ENI

content.goal: Goal: Create a VPC Flow Log for one network interface and view records in CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3.
content.title: Configure VPC Flow Logs for an ENI

values.label: Required permissions summary
values.value: STS identity check, ENI read access, Flow Logs, CloudWatch Logs, optional S3, IAM role setup, and cleanup.

cleanup.text: Delete subnets, route tables, Internet Gateways, and the custom VPC created during this lab.

cliSteps.note: Expected: you see your AWS account ID and ARN.
cliSteps.title: Check your AWS identity
cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: you see your AWS account ID and ARN.

cliSteps.note: Replace eni-replace-this with your test ENI ID.
cliSteps.title: Set variables

commands.text:
REGION=eu-west-2
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)
LOG_GROUP=/aws/vpc/task9/flowlogs
ROLE_NAME=saa-vpc-task9-flowlogs-role
ENI_ID=eni-replace-this

cliSteps.note: Wait about 20 seconds before creating the flow log so IAM can propagate.
cliSteps.title: Create CloudWatch log group and IAM role

commands.text:
aws logs create-log-group --log-group-name $LOG_GROUP --region $REGION
cat > trust-flowlogs.json <<'EOF'
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Principal":{"Service":"vpc-flow-logs.amazonaws.com"},"Action":"sts:AssumeRole"}]}
EOF
ROLE_ARN=$(aws iam create-role --role-name $ROLE_NAME --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-flowlogs.json --query 'Role.Arn' --output text)
cat > flowlogs-cw-policy.json <<EOF
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow","Action":["logs:CreateLogStream","logs:PutLogEvents","logs:DescribeLogGroups","logs:DescribeLogStreams"],"Resource":"arn:aws:logs:$REGION:$ACCOUNT_ID:log-group:$LOG_GROUP:*"}]}
EOF
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name $ROLE_NAME --policy-name saa-vpc-task9-flowlogs-cw --policy-document file://flowlogs-cw-policy.json

cliSteps.note: Expected: a Flow Log ID starts with fl-.
cliSteps.title: Create the ENI flow log

commands.text:
FLOW_LOG_ID=$(aws ec2 create-flow-logs --resource-type NetworkInterface --resource-ids $ENI_ID --traffic-type ALL --log-destination-type cloud-watch-logs --log-group-name $LOG_GROUP --deliver-logs-permission-arn $ROLE_ARN --region $REGION --query 'FlowLogIds[0]' --output text)
echo $FLOW_LOG_ID

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: a Flow Log ID starts with fl-.

cliSteps.note: Expected: status becomes ACTIVE. Log streams may take a few minutes.
cliSteps.title: Verify delivery

commands.text:
aws ec2 describe-flow-logs --flow-log-ids $FLOW_LOG_ID --region $REGION --query 'FlowLogs[0].FlowLogStatus'
aws logs describe-log-streams --log-group-name $LOG_GROUP --region $REGION --order-by LastEventTime --descending --max-items 5

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: status becomes ACTIVE. Log streams may take a few minutes.

cliSteps.title: CLI cleanup
cliSteps.warning: Delete the flow log before deleting the destination role.

commands.text:
aws ec2 delete-flow-logs --flow-log-ids $FLOW_LOG_ID --region $REGION
aws logs delete-log-group --log-group-name $LOG_GROUP --region $REGION
aws iam delete-role-policy --role-name $ROLE_NAME --policy-name saa-vpc-task9-flowlogs-cw
aws iam delete-role --role-name $ROLE_NAME
rm -f trust-flowlogs.json flowlogs-cw-policy.json

commands.text:
REGION=eu-west-2
TABLE_NAME=vpc-task25-books
VPC_ID=vpc-xxxxxxxx
ROUTE_TABLE_ID=rtb-xxxxxxxx
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)

aws dynamodb create-table --table-name $TABLE_NAME --attribute-definitions AttributeName=BookId,AttributeType=S --key-schema AttributeName=BookId,KeyType=HASH --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST --region $REGION
aws dynamodb wait table-exists --table-name $TABLE_NAME --region $REGION

VPCE_ID=$(aws ec2 create-vpc-endpoint --vpc-id $VPC_ID --service-name com.amazonaws.${REGION}.dynamodb --vpc-endpoint-type Gateway --route-table-ids $ROUTE_TABLE_ID --policy-document file://ddb-endpoint-policy.json --region $REGION --query 'VpcEndpoint.VpcEndpointId' --output text)
echo $VPCE_ID

commands.text:
VPC_ID=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.70.0.0/16 --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task7-vpc}]' --query 'Vpc.VpcId' --output text)
aws ec2 modify-vpc-attribute --vpc-id $VPC_ID --enable-dns-hostnames '{"Value":true}' --region $REGION
PUB_SUBNET=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC_ID --cidr-block 10.70.1.0/24 --availability-zone $AZ --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=task7-public-a}]' --query 'Subnet.SubnetId' --output text)
PRIV_SUBNET=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC_ID --cidr-block 10.70.11.0/24 --availability-zone $AZ --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=task7-private-a}]' --query 'Subnet.SubnetId' --output text)
IGW_ID=$(aws ec2 create-internet-gateway --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=internet-gateway,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task7-igw}]' --query 'InternetGateway.InternetGatewayId' --output text)
aws ec2 attach-internet-gateway --vpc-id $VPC_ID --internet-gateway-id $IGW_ID --region $REGION
RT_ID=$(aws ec2 create-route-table --vpc-id $VPC_ID --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=route-table,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=task7-public-rt}]' --query 'RouteTable.RouteTableId' --output text)
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $RT_ID --destination-cidr-block 0.0.0.0/0 --gateway-id $IGW_ID --region $REGION
ASSOC_ID=$(aws ec2 associate-route-table --route-table-id $RT_ID --subnet-id $PUB_SUBNET --region $REGION --query 'AssociationId' --output text)

commands.text:
NACL_ID=$(aws ec2 create-network-acl --vpc-id $VPC_ID --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=network-acl,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=task8-block-nacl}]' --query 'NetworkAcl.NetworkAclId' --output text)

NEW_ASSOC_ID=$(aws ec2 replace-network-acl-association --association-id $ASSOC_ID --network-acl-id $NACL_ID --region $REGION --query 'NewAssociationId' --output text)

content.goal: Goal: Peer two non-overlapping VPCs, add routes both ways, and test private IP connectivity.
content.title: Set up VPC peering and verify private connectivity

values.label: Required permissions summary
values.value: STS identity check, VPC setup, VPC peering, route tables, security groups, optional EC2 testing, and cleanup.

cleanup.text: Delete subnets, route tables, Internet Gateways, and the custom VPC created during this lab.

cliSteps.note: Expected: you see your AWS account ID and ARN.
cliSteps.title: Check your AWS identity
cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: you see your AWS account ID and ARN.

cliSteps.note: Expected: two VPCs with non-overlapping CIDRs.
cliSteps.title: Create VPCs and subnets

commands.text:
REGION=eu-west-2
AZ=eu-west-2a
VPC_A=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.100.0.0/16 --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task10-a}]' --query 'Vpc.VpcId' --output text)
VPC_B=$(aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.101.0.0/16 --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task10-b}]' --query 'Vpc.VpcId' --output text)
SUBNET_A=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC_A --cidr-block 10.100.1.0/24 --availability-zone $AZ --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=task10-a-private-a}]' --query 'Subnet.SubnetId' --output text)
SUBNET_B=$(aws ec2 create-subnet --vpc-id $VPC_B --cidr-block 10.101.1.0/24 --availability-zone $AZ --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=subnet,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=task10-b-private-a}]' --query 'Subnet.SubnetId' --output text)

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: two VPCs with non-overlapping CIDRs.

cliSteps.note: Expected: peering status becomes active after a short wait.
cliSteps.title: Create and accept peering

commands.text:
PCX_ID=$(aws ec2 create-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-id $VPC_A --peer-vpc-id $VPC_B --region $REGION --tag-specifications 'ResourceType=vpc-peering-connection,Tags=[{Key=Name,Value=saa-vpc-task10-peering}]' --query 'VpcPeeringConnection.VpcPeeringConnectionId' --output text)
aws ec2 accept-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-peering-connection-id $PCX_ID --region $REGION

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: peering status becomes active after a short wait.

cliSteps.note: VPCCIDRSubnetRoute destinationRoute targetVPC A10.100.0.0/1610.100.1.0/2410.101.0.0/16Peering connectionVPC B10.101.0.0/1610.101.1.0/2410.100.0.0/16Peering connection
cliSteps.title: Add routes both ways

commands.text:
RT_A=$(aws ec2 describe-route-tables --region $REGION --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_A --query 'RouteTables[0].RouteTableId' --output text)
RT_B=$(aws ec2 describe-route-tables --region $REGION --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_B --query 'RouteTables[0].RouteTableId' --output text)
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $RT_A --destination-cidr-block 10.101.0.0/16 --vpc-peering-connection-id $PCX_ID --region $REGION
aws ec2 create-route --route-table-id $RT_B --destination-cidr-block 10.100.0.0/16 --vpc-peering-connection-id $PCX_ID --region $REGION

cliSteps.note: Expected: ICMP is allowed only from the peer VPC CIDR.
cliSteps.title: Create security groups for private test traffic

commands.text:
SG_A=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name task10-a-sg --description 'Task 10 VPC A SG' --vpc-id $VPC_A --region $REGION --query 'GroupId' --output text)
SG_B=$(aws ec2 create-security-group --group-name task10-b-sg --description 'Task 10 VPC B SG' --vpc-id $VPC_B --region $REGION --query 'GroupId' --output text)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $SG_A --protocol icmp --port -1 --cidr 10.101.0.0/16 --region $REGION
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id $SG_B --protocol icmp --port -1 --cidr 10.100.0.0/16 --region $REGION

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: ICMP is allowed only from the peer VPC CIDR.

cliSteps.note: Expected: peering is active and both route tables have peer CIDR routes.
cliSteps.title: Verify peering and routes

commands.text:
aws ec2 describe-vpc-peering-connections --vpc-peering-connection-ids $PCX_ID --region $REGION --query 'VpcPeeringConnections[0].Status.Code'
aws ec2 describe-route-tables --route-table-ids $RT_A $RT_B --region $REGION --query 'RouteTables[*].Routes[*].{Destination:DestinationCidrBlock,Peering:VpcPeeringConnectionId,State:State}'

cliSteps.expectedResult: Expected: peering is active and both route tables have peer CIDR routes.

cliSteps.title: CLI cleanup
cliSteps.warning: Terminate test instances before running cleanup.

commands.text:
aws ec2 delete-route --route-table-id $RT_A --destination-cidr-block 10.101.0.0/16 --region $REGION
aws ec2 delete-route --route-table-id $RT_B --destination-cidr-block 10.100.0.0/16 --region $REGION
aws ec2 delete-vpc-peering-connection --vpc-peering-connection-id $PCX_ID --region $REGION
aws ec2 delete-security-group --group-id $SG_A --region $REGION
aws ec2 delete-security-group --group-id $SG_B --region $REGION
aws ec2 delete-subnet --subnet-id $SUBNET_A --region $REGION
aws ec2 delete-subnet --subnet-id $SUBNET_B --region $REGION
aws ec2 delete-vpc --vpc-id $VPC_A --region $REGION
aws ec2 delete-vpc --vpc-id $VPC_B --region $REGION

IP address: enter your on-prem router public IP.

ASN: use Amazon default ASN for this lab.

consoleSteps.title: Create the Site-to-Site VPN connection

instructions.text: Open VPC → Site-to-Site VPN connections.
Choose Create VPN connection.
Target gateway type: Virtual private gateway.
Customer gateway: choose saa-vpc-task17-cgw.
Routing options: choose Static and add 192.168.10.0/24.

consoleSteps.note: The return route must also exist on the on-prem router.

instructions.text: Open VPC → Route tables.
Select the private subnet route table.
Choose Routes → Edit routes.
Add destination 192.168.10.0/24 and target the virtual private gateway.

consoleSteps.warning: Security groups, NACLs, firewalls, and the on-prem router must all allow the test traffic.
